text: What is the Central Limit Theorem (CLT) and why is it foundational to inferential statistics?
idealAnswer: The Central Limit Theorem states that as sample size n becomes sufficiently large (typically n >= 30), the sampling distribution of the sample mean approaches a Gaussian normal distribution regardless of the underlying population distribution shape, provided samples are independent and identically distributed with finite variance.

conditions.name: Sampling Distribution Convergence to Normal Distribution

text: What is a p-value in hypothesis testing, and how does it relate to the significance level alpha?
idealAnswer: A p-value is the probability of observing test results at least as extreme as the observed sample data, assuming the null hypothesis (H0) is strictly true. If the p-value is less than or equal to the pre-determined significance level alpha (commonly 0.05), we reject the null hypothesis in favor of the alternative hypothesis.

conditions.name: Probability of Observing Extreme Data Given Null Hypothesis
Significance Threshold Alpha (0.05) Comparison

text: Explain the difference between Type I and Type II errors in statistical hypothesis testing.
idealAnswer: A Type I error (false positive) occurs when we reject a null hypothesis that is actually true, with probability equal to significance level alpha. A Type II error (false negative) occurs when we fail to reject a false null hypothesis, with probability beta. Statistical power (1 - beta) represents the probability of correctly rejecting a false null hypothesis.

conditions.name: Type I Error (False Positive) and Alpha Relationship
Type II Error (False Negative) and Beta Probability

text: How do you detect and handle outliers in a continuous numerical feature distribution?
idealAnswer: Outliers can be detected using statistical boundaries: the Interquartile Range (IQR) method flags points outside [Q1 - 1.5*IQR, Q3 + 1.5*IQR], while Z-score flags points with absolute standard deviation > 3 for Gaussian distributions. Handling strategies include data verification, Winsorizing (capping percentiles), log/power transformations, or robust non-parametric models like tree ensembles.

Z-score Standard Deviation Thresholding

text: What are the core Gauss-Markov assumptions of Ordinary Least Squares (OLS) Linear Regression?
idealAnswer: OLS assumes: linearity in parameters, random sampling of data, no perfect multicollinearity among predictors, zero conditional mean of errors (exogeneity: E(u|x) = 0), homoscedasticity (constant error variance across predictor levels), and no auto-correlation among error residuals.

Exogeneity (Zero Conditional Mean of Residuals)
Homoscedasticity and Error Independence

text: Explain the ROC curve and the Area Under the Curve (AUC-ROC) metric for binary classifiers.
idealAnswer: The Receiver Operating Characteristic (ROC) curve plots True Positive Rate (Sensitivity/Recall) on the y-axis against False Positive Rate (1 - Specificity) on the x-axis across all classification probability thresholds from 0 to 1. The AUC-ROC measures the two-dimensional area under this curve, quantifying the probability that the classifier ranks a randomly chosen positive sample higher than a randomly chosen negative sample, where 0.5 is random chance and 1.0 is perfect separation.

conditions.name: TPR vs FPR Across All Classification Thresholds
Area Under Curve (AUC) Probability Ranking Interpretation
Threshold-Invariance and Class Distribution Robustness

text: What is Principal Component Analysis (PCA) and how does it reduce feature dimensionality while preserving variance?
idealAnswer: PCA is an unsupervised linear dimensionality reduction technique that transforms correlated features into a smaller set of orthogonal, uncorrelated axes called principal components. It standardizes data, computes the covariance matrix, and performs eigendecomposition (or SVD) to find eigenvectors that maximize variance along successive orthogonal directions, projecting high-dimensional data onto the top-k components.

conditions.name: Covariance Matrix and Orthogonal Eigenvector Decomposition
Variance Maximization on Successive Projection Axes

text: Explain the K-Means clustering algorithm, the role of inertia, and the Elbow method for choosing k.
idealAnswer: K-Means partitions n samples into k clusters by iteratively: assigning each point to its nearest centroid based on Euclidean distance, and recalculating centroids as the arithmetic mean of all assigned points until convergence. Inertia measures within-cluster sum of squares (WCSS). The Elbow method plots inertia across various k values, selecting the inflection point (elbow) where diminishing returns in variance reduction occur.

conditions.name: Centroid Assignment and Mean Recalculation Iteration
Inertia and Within-Cluster Sum of Squares (WCSS)
Elbow Method and Inflection Point Selection

text: What is Data Leakage in machine learning, and how does improper feature preprocessing cause it?
idealAnswer: Data leakage occurs when information from outside the training dataset (specifically target or validation/test data) inadvertently influences model training, producing artificially inflated validation scores that fail to generalize to production. A classic cause is performing feature scaling, imputation, or target encoding on the full dataset before splitting into train/test sets, rather than fitting transformers strictly on training folds.

Full-Dataset Preprocessing Anti-pattern (Scaling/Imputation)

text: What are the core steps in designing and analyzing a basic online A/B experiment?
idealAnswer: Designing an A/B test involves: defining the primary metric (e.g. conversion rate), formulating null and alternative hypotheses, conducting power analysis to calculate required sample size and experiment duration, randomly splitting traffic into control (A) and treatment (B) variants to ensure no bias, and evaluating statistical significance via two-sample t-test or z-test post-experiment.

conditions.name: Hypothesis Formulation and Metric Selection
Statistical Power Analysis and Sample Size Sizing
Random Assignment and Two-Sample Significance Testing

text: Explain the difference between covariance and correlation, and why correlation does not imply causation.
idealAnswer: Covariance measures the joint directional variability of two random variables, but its magnitude depends on the units of measurement, making cross-dataset comparisons difficult. Pearson correlation is normalized covariance divided by the product of their standard deviations, bounded strictly between -1 and +1. Correlation does not imply causation because observed relationships may be driven by confounding variables, reverse causality, or pure coincidence.

text: Compare One-Hot Encoding with Target Encoding for categorical variables in high-cardinality datasets.
idealAnswer: One-Hot Encoding converts each categorical category into a binary column, which causes the curse of dimensionality and memory bloat on high-cardinality features (e.g. ZIP codes with 40,000 values). Target (Mean) Encoding replaces categories with the mean target value for that category, retaining a single compact column, but requires smoothing and cross-fold regularization to prevent severe target leakage and overfitting.

text: What is stationarity in time series analysis, and why is it required for ARIMA modeling?
idealAnswer: A time series is strictly stationary (or weakly stationary) if its statistical properties—specifically mean, variance, and autocovariance—are constant over time and independent of time t. ARIMA modeling requires stationarity because forecasting algorithms assume future behavior follows past statistical distributions; non-stationary series exhibiting trends or seasonality must be differenced (d parameter in ARIMA) or transformed.

conditions.name: Constant Mean and Variance Over Time Definition
Differencing and Transformation for Non-stationary Series
Statistical Testing for Stationarity (ADF Test)

text: What are SHAP values, and how do they use game theory to explain individual machine learning predictions?
idealAnswer: SHAP (SHapley Additive exPlanations) values assign each feature an importance value for a specific model prediction, rooted in cooperative game theory (Shapley values). It evaluates the marginal contribution of a feature across all possible feature coalitions, satisfying fairness properties like local accuracy, missingness, and consistency, allowing granular local and global model interpretability.

text: How do Propensity Score Matching (PSM) and Difference-in-Differences (DiD) estimate causal treatment effects in observational data?
idealAnswer: When randomized controlled trials are impossible, observational data suffers from confounding selection bias. Propensity Score Matching estimates the conditional probability of receiving treatment given baseline covariates via logistic regression, pairing treated and control units with similar propensity scores to balance confounders. Difference-in-Differences estimates causal effects across longitudinal data by comparing changes over time between treatment and control groups, relying on the parallel trends assumption.

conditions.name: Selection Bias and Confounder Imbalance in Observational Studies

text: What is the Multiple Testing Problem in statistical analysis, and how do Bonferroni and Benjamini-Hochberg (FDR) corrections handle it?
idealAnswer: When testing m simultaneous hypotheses at alpha=0.05, the cumulative probability of at least one false positive (Family-Wise Error Rate) inflates to 1 - (1 - alpha)^m. The Bonferroni correction controls FWER strictly by testing each hypothesis at alpha/m, but is overly conservative, causing high Type II errors. The Benjamini-Hochberg procedure controls the False Discovery Rate (FDR)—the expected proportion of false positives among all rejected hypotheses—offering higher statistical power.

conditions.name: Family-Wise Error Rate (FWER) Alpha Inflation
Bonferroni Conservative Threshold Scaling (alpha/m)
Benjamini-Hochberg False Discovery Rate (FDR) Control

text: What is Multicollinearity, how does Variance Inflation Factor (VIF) detect it, and what are its remedies?
idealAnswer: Multicollinearity occurs when two or more independent predictor variables in a multiple regression model are highly linearly correlated, causing unstable coefficient estimates, inflated standard errors, and wide confidence intervals. Variance Inflation Factor (VIF = 1 / (1 - R_i^2)) measures how much coefficient variance is inflated due to collinearity; VIF > 5 or 10 indicates severe multicollinearity, remedied by removing collinear features, feature engineering (PCA), or applying L2 Ridge regression.

conditions.name: Inflated Standard Errors and Unstable Coefficient Estimates
Variance Inflation Factor (VIF) Mathematical Detection
Remediation Strategies (Ridge Regularization, PCA, Feature Pruning)

text: Compare t-SNE and UMAP for non-linear high-dimensional data visualization and clustering.
idealAnswer: t-SNE models pairwise similarities as conditional probabilities under Gaussian distributions in high-dimensional space and Student-t distributions in low-dimensional space, minimizing Kullback-Leibler divergence; it preserves local neighbor structures well but destroys global geometry and scales poorly O(N^2). UMAP models Riemannian manifold fuzzy simplicial sets, preserving both local neighborhoods and superior global cluster topology with much faster O(N log N) scalability.

conditions.name: t-SNE Probabilistic Distance and Student-t Distribution
UMAP Manifold Fuzzy Simplicial Sets and Global Topology
Computational Scalability and Hyperparameter Differences

text: Explain SMOTE (Synthetic Minority Over-sampling Technique) and how it generates synthetic data without simple duplication.
idealAnswer: Simple random oversampling duplicates minority samples, which increases overfitting risks without adding new information. SMOTE synthesizes new minority samples along feature space lines connecting k-nearest neighbors: for each minority instance x, it finds its k-nearest minority neighbors, selects one at random x_zi, and creates a synthetic instance x_new = x + lambda * (x_zi - x), where lambda is a uniform random number between 0 and 1.

conditions.name: Oversampling Duplication Overfitting Drawbacks

text: What is Variance Reduction in A/B testing using CUPED (Controlled-Experiment Using Pre-Experiment Data)?
idealAnswer: CUPED uses pre-experiment metric data X (correlated with experiment metric Y) to remove known pre-existing variance: Y_cuped = Y - theta * (X - E[X]), where optimal theta = Cov(Y, X) / Var(X). This reduces variance by a factor of (1 - rho^2), where rho is the correlation between pre and post metrics. Lower variance shrinks standard errors, enabling teams to achieve required statistical power with up to 50% smaller sample sizes or shorter runtimes.

conditions.name: Pre-experiment Covariate Regression Formulation
Mathematical Variance Reduction Factor (1 - rho^2)
Business Impact: Sample Size Shrinkage and Fast Iteration

text: Compare Frequentist and Bayesian statistical inference, detailing Priors, Likelihood, and Posterior distributions.
idealAnswer: Frequentist inference treats parameters as fixed, unknown constants and probabilities as long-run frequencies over infinite hypothetical repetitions. Bayesian inference treats parameters as random variables with probability distributions reflecting uncertainty. Bayes Theorem updates Prior beliefs P(theta) using the Likelihood of observed data P(D|theta) to compute the Posterior distribution P(theta|D) = (P(D|theta) * P(theta)) / P(D).

Bayes Theorem Prior, Likelihood, and Posterior Components
Credible Intervals vs Frequentist Confidence Intervals

text: Explain Autoregressive Integrated Moving Average (ARIMA) and how ACF and PACF plots identify p, d, q parameters.
idealAnswer: ARIMA(p, d, q) models non-stationary time series by combining Autoregression of order p (regression on past lags), Differencing of degree d (to achieve stationarity), and Moving Average of order q (linear combination of past white-noise forecast errors). The Autocorrelation Function (ACF) plot identifies MA order q from the lag after which autocorrelations cut off; the Partial Autocorrelation Function (PACF) identifies AR order p from the lag after which partial correlations cut off.

text: How do you evaluate clustering quality without ground truth labels using Silhouette Score and Davies-Bouldin Index?
idealAnswer: In unsupervised clustering, internal validation metrics quantify cluster separation and compactness. The Silhouette Score s(i) = (b(i) - a(i)) / max(a(i), b(i)) compares intra-cluster distance a(i) with nearest-cluster distance b(i), bounded between -1 (misclustered) and +1 (dense, well-separated). The Davies-Bouldin Index calculates the similarity between each cluster and its most similar peer as the ratio of within-cluster scatter to between-cluster separation; lower Davies-Bouldin values indicate better clustering.

conditions.name: Silhouette Score Formulation (a vs b Distances)

text: Compare Logistic Loss (Log-Loss) with Hinge Loss in binary classification, detailing margin optimization.
idealAnswer: Logistic Loss (Binary Cross-Entropy) models probabilistic class likelihoods, penalizing predictions continuously with smooth gradients even when correctly classified, encouraging confident probability calibration. Hinge Loss (max(0, 1 - y * f(x))) is utilized in Support Vector Machines, imposing zero penalty for points correctly classified beyond the margin threshold (y * f(x) >= 1), creating sparse support vectors and focusing strictly on decision boundary maximization rather than calibrated probabilities.

conditions.name: Log-Loss Probabilistic Smooth Continuous Optimization
Hinge Loss Maximum Margin and Zero-Penalty Flat Region
Support Vectors Sparsity vs Probability Calibration Trade-off

text: What is Bootstrapping in non-parametric statistics, and how does it generate empirical confidence intervals?
idealAnswer: Bootstrapping is a resampling technique that approximates the sampling distribution of an estimator by drawing B replacement samples of size n from the original observed dataset. By computing the target statistic on each bootstrap replicate, we build an empirical distribution, allowing construction of confidence intervals (such as percentile or BCa intervals) and standard error estimates without making parametric distributional assumptions.

text: What are Network Spillover Effects in marketplace A/B tests (e.g. Uber/Airbnb) and how do Cluster-Based Randomization mitigate them?
idealAnswer: In two-sided marketplace platforms, user-level A/B testing suffers from network interference (SUTVA violation): treating one rider or seller affects supply and price for control riders in the same geography. Cluster-based randomization mitigates spillovers by randomizing intact geographical clusters (e.g. entire cities or grid zones) or temporal switchback windows (alternating treatment/control by hour across the entire market), containing treatment interactions within the cluster.

conditions.name: SUTVA Violation and Cannibalization / Supply Interference
Cluster-Based Spatial Randomization Design
Temporal Switchback Experimentation Protocols

text: Explain Weight of Evidence (WoE) and Information Value (IV) in credit scoring and logistic regression modeling.
idealAnswer: Weight of Evidence (WoE) recodes categorical or binned continuous variables into linear log-odds: WoE_i = ln(% Goods / % Bads), transforming non-linear relationships into a monotonic linear scale with respect to the logit target. Information Value (IV = sum((% Goods - % Bads) * WoE)) quantifies the overall predictive strength of a feature, used to rank and filter features (<0.02 useless, 0.1-0.3 medium, >0.5 suspiciously high/overfitting).

conditions.name: Weight of Evidence Log-Odds Formulation
Information Value Predictive Ranking Formulation
Credit Risk Modeling and Monotonic Transformation

text: How does Survival Analysis handle right-censored event data using the Kaplan-Meier estimator and Cox Proportional Hazards model?
idealAnswer: Standard regression fails on time-to-event data because some subjects have not experienced the event by the study conclusion (right-censoring). The Kaplan-Meier non-parametric estimator calculates survival probabilities at each observed event time, properly incorporating censored subjects up to their last observation. The Cox Proportional Hazards semi-parametric model estimates the impact of covariates on hazard rates (h(t) = h0(t) * exp(beta*X)) under the assumption of constant hazard ratios over time.

conditions.name: Right-Censoring and Incomplete Observation Mechanics
Kaplan-Meier Non-Parametric Survival Curve Estimation
Cox Proportional Hazards and Hazard Ratio Assumption

text: Explain Bayesian Optimization for hyperparameter tuning using Gaussian Processes and Acquisition Functions (Expected Improvement).
idealAnswer: Bayesian Optimization finds the global maximum of expensive black-box objective functions by maintaining a Gaussian Process (GP) prior over objective functions. The GP provides both a posterior mean prediction mu(x) and uncertainty variance sigma(x) at any parameter coordinate. Acquisition functions like Expected Improvement (EI) or Upper Confidence Bound (UCB) balance exploration (high uncertainty sigma) and exploitation (high predicted mean mu) to sample the next optimal evaluation point with minimal objective evaluations.

conditions.name: Gaussian Process Surrogate Model Posterior Distribution
Exploration vs Exploitation Trade-off Formulation

text: How does the Metropolis-Hastings MCMC algorithm sample from unnormalized posterior probability distributions?
idealAnswer: When posterior distributions have intractable high-dimensional normalization integrals (the denominator P(D) in Bayes rule), Metropolis-Hastings generates a stationary Markov chain whose equilibrium distribution matches the target posterior. At step t, a candidate state x_star is proposed from transition density q(x_star | x_t) and accepted with probability alpha = min(1, [P(x_star)*q(x_t|x_star)] / [P(x_t)*q(x_star|x_t)]). Because P(x) appears in numerator and denominator, intractable normalization constants cancel out.

conditions.name: Intractable Normalization Constant (Evidence Integral) Challenge
Proposal Distribution Transition and Acceptance Ratio Alpha
Stationary Distribution Convergence and Burn-in Period

text: Explain the Curse of Dimensionality and its geometric implications on distances and data sparsity in high-dimensional spaces.
idealAnswer: As dimension d increases, the volume of a hypersphere of radius r relative to a bounding hypercube of edge 2r approaches zero (volume concentrated in corners). Data points become exponentially sparse, requiring exponential sample sizes to maintain density. Furthermore, distance metrics concentrate: the distance between the nearest and furthest neighbors approaches zero in relative terms ((d_max - d_min) / d_min -> 0), rendering Euclidean distance metrics ineffective for clustering and classification.

conditions.name: Hypercube Corner Volume Concentration and Exponential Sparsity
Distance Concentration Phenomenon ((d_max - d_min) / d_min -> 0)
Mitigation via Manifold Learning and Regularized Projections

text: How does Extreme Value Theory (EVT) model rare tail risks using Block Maxima and Peaks Over Threshold (POT)?
idealAnswer: Standard Gaussian statistics underestimate heavy-tailed events. Extreme Value Theory characterizes the asymptotic distribution of tail extremes. The Block Maxima approach divides observations into equal time blocks (e.g. years) and models block maximums using the Generalized Extreme Value (GEV) distribution (Gumbel, Frechet, Weibull). The Peaks Over Threshold (POT) approach models all observations exceeding a high threshold u using the Generalized Pareto Distribution (GPD), enabling estimation of extreme Value at Risk (VaR) and Expected Shortfall.

conditions.name: Heavy-Tailed Risk Underestimation of Gaussian Assumptions

text: Explain d-separation, back-door criterion, and Judea Pearl do-calculus for causal effect identification in DAGs.
idealAnswer: In Directed Acyclic Graphs (DAGs), d-separation determines whether two nodes X and Y are conditionally independent given set Z by checking active paths across chains, forks, and colliders (where conditioning on a collider opens the path). Pearl Back-Door Criterion identifies a set of variables Z that blocks all spurious non-causal paths between X and Y without conditioning on descendants of X. Do-calculus P(Y | do(X)) maps physical interventions to observational distributions by severing incoming arrows to X.

conditions.name: d-separation, Colliders, Forks, and Chains in DAGs

Do-Calculus Interventional Distribution Identification

text: How do Sequential Probability Ratio Tests (SPRT) allow continuous monitoring in A/B testing without inflating false positive rates?
idealAnswer: Repeatedly checking p-values during an A/B test (peeking) drastically inflates false positive rates beyond nominal alpha. Wald Sequential Probability Ratio Test (SPRT) computes the cumulative log-likelihood ratio of data under alternative vs null hypotheses after each observation. The test continuously evaluates boundaries: if the ratio exceeds upper threshold A, reject H0; if it falls below lower threshold B, accept H0; otherwise continue sampling. This guarantees exact Type I and Type II error rates while stopping early on large treatment effects.

conditions.name: Peeking Problem and Continuous P-Value Checking Inflation
Wald Cumulative Log-Likelihood Ratio Updating Protocol
Stopping Boundaries (A and B) and Sample Size Efficiency

text: Explain Kullback-Leibler (KL) Divergence, Cross-Entropy, and Mutual Information in statistical learning.
idealAnswer: Entropy H(P) = -sum(P(x)*log P(x)) measures the fundamental uncertainty of a probability distribution. Cross-Entropy H(P, Q) = -sum(P(x)*log Q(x)) measures the expected coding length when using approximate distribution Q to encode true distribution P. KL Divergence D_KL(P || Q) = H(P, Q) - H(P) quantifies the information loss (relative entropy) from approximating P with Q, non-negative by Gibbs inequality. Mutual Information I(X; Y) = D_KL(P(X,Y) || P(X)P(Y)) measures mutual statistical dependence.

conditions.name: Shannon Entropy and Information Uncertainty Definition
Cross-Entropy and KL Divergence Relative Entropy Formulation
Mutual Information Non-Linear Dependence Quantification

text: Explain the Expectation-Maximization (EM) algorithm and its mathematical convergence proof via Jensen Inequality.
idealAnswer: The Expectation-Maximization algorithm estimates maximum likelihood parameters in latent variable models (e.g. Gaussian Mixture Models). In the E-step, it computes the expected value of the complete-data log-likelihood with respect to the posterior distribution of latent variables given current parameters. In the M-step, it maximizes this expectation to update parameters. By Jensen inequality on the convex logarithm, each EM iteration maximizes an Evidence Lower Bound (ELBO), guaranteeing monotonic convergence to local likelihood maxima.

conditions.name: Latent Variable Models and Incomplete Data Log-Likelihood
E-Step Expectation Calculation and M-Step Parameter Maximization
Jensen Inequality and ELBO Monotonic Convergence Proof
